your integration tests almost certainly hit Stripe's test endpoints under normal latency, not the timeout/retry race condition itself

When an SDK retries a request after a timeout, it doesn't actually know whether the original request succeeded server-side — the timeout could mean "no response received" while the charge still went through. If retries aren't scoped by an idempotency key on every payment-mutating call (create charge, create payment intent, capture, etc.), turning on retry-by-default can turn "network hiccup during a flash sale" into "customer charged twice." [...] CI/integration tests passing doesn't catch this. Those tests almost never simulate a slow/timing-out gateway response with a real retry firing — they test the happy path and maybe explicit error codes, not the timeout race condition.

If the SDK retries that call automatically and it isn't scoped to safe/idempotent operations (or doesn't attach an idempotency key itself), you can end up double-charging customers... Most integration suites hit a sandbox that responds normally; they won't catch this unless someone specifically wrote a test that simulates a slow/dropped response.

Does the checkout code already pass an explicit idempotency key on charge/payment-intent creation calls? If yes, this is much lower risk (retries just reuse the same key, Stripe dedupes). If no, this bump could introduce duplicate charges... Green CI and passing "payment integration tests" almost certainly don't cover this. Testing retry-under-timeout requires injecting a slow/timing-out response and asserting no duplicate charge occurs — that's a specific fault-injection test, not something a normal happy-path integration suite exercises.

The real risk isn't the diff size, it's the behavior change buried in the changelog. "Automatic retries on timeout" for a payment SDK is not a minor resilience win by default — it's a duplicate-charge risk. If a request to create a charge/payment intent times out on the client side but actually succeeded server-side, a naive retry sends a second charge request.

If `stripe-node-lite` now retries those calls automatically and your checkout service's charge/payment-intent calls aren't passing idempotency keys, this upgrade introduces a live risk of **duplicate charges**... Green CI / payment integration tests: these almost certainly test the happy path and maybe explicit error handling, not "what happens when a request times out after Stripe already processed it and the SDK retries."
